diseases.name: Melanoma
diseases.short_description: A serious form of skin cancer arising from melanocytes (pigment-producing cells). Characterized by asymmetry, irregular borders, and color variability.
common_characteristics: Asymmetry: One half of the spot does not match the other half
Border irregularity: Edges are ragged, notched, blurred, or poorly defined
Color variation: Shades of brown, black, sometimes with patches of pink, red, white, or blue
Diameter: Typically greater than 6 mm, though can be smaller in early stages
Evolving: Changing in size, shape, color, or elevation over time
diagnostic_approaches: Clinical dermoscopy evaluating pigment network, atypical dots/globules, and blue-white veil
Excisional biopsy with narrow margins for formal histopathological examination
Microscopic Breslow thickness and ulceration assessment
Sentinel lymph node biopsy for deeper or higher-risk lesions
treatment_approaches: Wide local surgical excision with clear histological margins
Lymph node dissection when regional metastasis is suspected or confirmed
Immunotherapy (checkpoint inhibitors such as PD-1 or CTLA-4 inhibitors)
Targeted therapy for lesions harboring BRAF V600 mutations
Adjuvant radiotherapy in select high-risk or advanced scenarios
diseases.when_to_seek_care: Promptly consult a dermatologist if any existing mole changes in size, shape, or color, if a new persistent pigmented lesion develops, or if a lesion bleeds, itches, or fails to heal.
sources: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) Melanoma Guidelines
World Health Organization (WHO) Skin Cancer Advisory

diseases.name: Melanocytic Nevi
diseases.short_description: Common benign skin growths composed of clustered melanocytes, commonly known as moles. Usually harmless and stable in appearance.
common_characteristics: Symmetrical round or oval shape with smooth, well-demarcated margins
Uniform pigmentation, typically ranging from tan to dark brown
Can be flat (junctional), slightly raised (compound), or dome-shaped (intradermal)
Usually stable over long periods once adulthood is reached
diagnostic_approaches: Dermoscopic assessment revealing regular, uniform pigment networks or homogenous patterns
Digital dermoscopy surveillance for individuals with dysplastic or multiple nevi
Diagnostic biopsy only if architectural atypia or suspicious evolution is noted
treatment_approaches: Clinical observation and routine sun protection; no treatment needed for benign nevi
Elective surgical excision or shave biopsy if mechanically irritated or cosmetically desired
Histological examination if removed to verify absence of dysplasia or malignancy
diseases.when_to_seek_care: Seek medical review if a mole develops the ABCDE warning signs (Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color changes, Diameter >6mm, Evolution) or becomes symptomatic.

diseases.name: Basal Cell Carcinoma
diseases.short_description: The most common form of skin cancer. Arises in the basal layer of the epidermis, typically slow-growing and rarely metastasizing, but locally destructive if untreated.
common_characteristics: Translucent, pearly, or waxy papule or nodule often with rolled borders
Visible branching blood vessels (arborizing telangiectasia) across the surface
Central ulceration, crusted depression, or persistent non-healing sore
Commonly located on chronically sun-exposed areas (face, ears, neck, scalp)
diagnostic_approaches: Dermoscopy identifying arborizing telangiectasia, leaf-like structures, or blue-gray ovoid nests
Punch, shave, or incisional skin biopsy to confirm histological subtype
Clinical mapping of lesion margins before definitive excision
treatment_approaches: Standard surgical excision with 4–5 mm clear margins
Mohs micrographic surgery for high-risk, recurrent, or cosmetically sensitive facial sites
Electrodesiccation and curettage for small superficial low-risk lesions
Topical therapy (imiquimod, 5-FU) or photodynamic therapy for selected superficial BCCs
Targeted oral Hedgehog pathway inhibitors for locally advanced or inoperable cases
diseases.when_to_seek_care: Consult a healthcare provider for any shiny bump, pink growth, or sore that bleeds easily, crusts over, or persists for more than 3 to 4 weeks.
sources: National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) Guidelines for BCC

diseases.name: Actinic Keratoses & Intraepithelial Carcinoma
diseases.short_description: Rough, scaly patches caused by chronic ultraviolet light exposure. Considered precancerous lesions that can potentially progress to invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC).
common_characteristics: Dry, rough, gritty, or sandpaper-like texture on sun-damaged skin
Flat or slightly raised red, pink, or brownish scaly plaques
Often more easily felt by light palpation than observed visually
Frequent on face, balding scalp, ears, forearms, and backs of hands
diagnostic_approaches: Clinical tactile and dermoscopic examination revealing 'strawberry' or rosette patterns
Dermatopathology biopsy if lesion is indurated, tender, or exhibits significant hyperkeratosis
treatment_approaches: Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen for isolated individual lesions
Field-directed topical therapy (5-fluorouracil, imiquimod cream, or tirbanibulin)
Photodynamic therapy (PDT) for extensive sun-damaged fields
Curettage or surgical excision if progression to invasive SCC is suspected
diseases.when_to_seek_care: Schedule a medical evaluation for scaly patches that persist, thicken, become tender, or develop elevated ulcerated borders.

diseases.name: Benign Keratosis-like Lesions
diseases.short_description: Non-cancerous skin conditions including seborrheic keratoses, solar lentigines, and lichen planus-like keratoses. Very common with advancing age.
common_characteristics: Waxy, scaly, or 'stuck-on' appearance sitting on the skin surface
Color ranges from light tan and yellow to deep brown or black
Well-demarcated edges with a granular, verrucous, or velvety surface
Completely benign with no intrinsic malignant transformation potential
diagnostic_approaches: Dermoscopy revealing characteristic comedo-like openings, milia-like cysts, and hairpin vessels
Shave biopsy performed if heavily pigmented and clinically mimicking melanoma
treatment_approaches: Reassurance and clinical observation; therapeutic intervention is not medically required
Cryosurgery, shave removal, or curettage if irritated by clothing or cosmetically bothersome
Electrocautery for small pedunculated or superficial lesions
diseases.when_to_seek_care: Consult a doctor if a lesion rapidly darkens, develops asymmetric growth, bleeds spontaneously, or cannot be reliably distinguished from melanoma.

diseases.name: Dermatofibroma
diseases.short_description: A common, harmless cutaneous nodule composed of fibrous tissue and histiocytes, often arising secondary to minor trauma or insect bites.
common_characteristics: Firm, button-like solitary nodule typically felt within the dermis
Color varies from pink and reddish-brown to dark tan
Positive 'dimple sign': dimples inward when squeezed laterally between thumb and forefinger
Most commonly located on lower legs of young to middle-aged adults
diagnostic_approaches: Clinical palpatory assessment and elicitation of the dimple sign
Dermoscopy classically showing a central white scar-like patch with a delicate peripheral pigment network
Biopsy reserved for atypical, growing, or painful variants
treatment_approaches: Reassurance; no treatment is necessary as lesions are completely benign
Complete simple surgical excision if symptomatic, repeatedly traumatized, or cosmetically undesired
Superficial cryotherapy to flatten raised contours
diseases.when_to_seek_care: Seek clinical evaluation if a firm nodule changes rapidly, bleeds, becomes painful, or lacks characteristic benign dermoscopic features.

diseases.name: Vascular Lesions
diseases.short_description: Non-cancerous proliferations of blood vessels including cherry angiomas, angiokeratomas, and pyogenic granulomas.
common_characteristics: Bright red, purple, or violaceous macules, papules, or small nodules
Blanching or partial blanching under diascopy (pressure from a glass slide)
Smooth or dome-shaped surface with well-defined borders
Common cherry angiomas multiply harmlessly with age on the trunk and limbs
diagnostic_approaches: Clinical inspection and diascopy assessment
Dermoscopy revealing red, purple, or blue-black round lacunae (vascular lagoons)
Biopsy indicated if lesion is thrombosed, dark, or mimics nodular melanoma
treatment_approaches: No treatment required for asymptomatic, stable benign lesions
Vascular laser therapy (pulsed dye laser, Nd:YAG) for cosmetic clearance
Electrocautery, curettage, or shave excision for bleeding pyogenic granulomas
diseases.when_to_seek_care: Consult a healthcare provider if a red spot bleeds profusely, turns black, grows rapidly, or causes recurrent discomfort.

diseases.name: Acne
diseases.short_description: A multifactorial inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous unit characterized by comedones, erythematous papules, pustules, and occasional nodules or cysts.
common_characteristics: Closed comedones (whiteheads) and open comedones (blackheads)
Inflammatory erythematous papules and superficial pustules
Occasional deeper tender nodules or pseudocysts in severe grades
Commonly localized to sebum-rich areas (face, chest, upper back)
Risk of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation or scarring
diagnostic_approaches: Clinical grading of lesion count and severity (PGA / GAGS scale)
Evaluation of comedonal vs. inflammatory predominant components
Assessment of contributing endocrinological factors (e.g., PCOS in females)
Screening for medication-induced acneiform eruptions
treatment_approaches: Topical retinoids (adapalene, tretinoin) for comedolytic regulation
Topical benzoyl peroxide and topical/oral antibiotics for inflammatory control
Oral isotretinoin for severe, recalcitrant, or scarring nodulocystic acne
Hormonal therapies (combined oral contraceptives, spironolactone)
Gentle non-comedogenic skincare and daily SPF sunscreen
diseases.when_to_seek_care: Consult a dermatologist if over-the-counter washes fail, if painful deep cysts or permanent scarring appear, or if acne significantly impacts emotional well-being.
sources: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) Acne Clinical Guidelines
British Association of Dermatologists (BAD) Acne Management Guidelines

diseases.name: Allergic Contact Dermatitis
diseases.short_description: An immunologically mediated delayed hypersensitivity eruption occurring after cutaneous exposure to an exogenous environmental allergen.
common_characteristics: Erythematous, intensely pruritic macules, plaques, and tiny vesicles
Well-demarcated geometric or artificial distribution matching contact zone
Oozing, crusting, and scaling in acute stages; lichenification in chronic phases
Latency period of 24–72 hours following exposure to sensitized contactant
diagnostic_approaches: Detailed exposure history (occupational, cosmetics, jewelry, plants)
Standardized cutaneous patch testing with baseline allergen series
Repeated Open Application Testing (ROAT) for leave-on products
Differential exclusion of irritant contact dermatitis and atopic dermatitis
treatment_approaches: Strict identification and permanent elimination of culprit allergens
Short-course mid-to-high potency topical corticosteroids for acute flares
Cool compresses and barrier restoration creams (ceramide-based emollients)
Short course of oral corticosteroids for widespread or facial involvement
Oral antihistamines for symptomatic control of intense pruritus
diseases.when_to_seek_care: Seek medical care if rash is widespread, involves the eyes/face/genitalia, shows yellow crusting indicating secondary infection, or fails to resolve with trigger elimination.
sources: American Contact Dermatitis Society (ACDS) Core Guidelines

diseases.name: Eczema (Atopic Dermatitis)
diseases.short_description: A chronic, relapsing, pruritic inflammatory skin disorder associated with epidermal barrier dysfunction (filaggrin mutations) and immune dysregulation.
common_characteristics: Intense itch (pruritus) leading to persistent scratch-itch cycle
Erythema, scaling, excoriations, and xerosis (severe dryness)
Classic flexural distribution (antecubital and popliteal fossae) in adults
Facial and extensor involvement common in infants and young children
Lichenification (thickened leather-like skin) from chronic rubbing
diagnostic_approaches: Hanifin and Rajka diagnostic criteria or UK Working Party criteria
Evaluation of personal or family history of atopic triad (asthma, allergic rhinitis)
Assessment of disease severity via EASI (Eczema Area and Severity Index) or SCORAD
Bacterial swab if honey-colored crusts suggest secondary Staphylococcal infection
treatment_approaches: Liberal daily application of lipid-rich barrier repair emollients
Intermittent proactive topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors
Topical PDE4 inhibitors (crisaborole) or JAK inhibitors for mild-moderate cases
Systemic biologics (dupilumab, tralokinumab) or JAK inhibitors for severe disease
Bleach baths or antiseptic cleansers to reduce Staphylococcus aureus colonization
diseases.when_to_seek_care: Consult a dermatologist if itching disturbs sleep, skin shows oozing/pus indicating bacterial infection, or sudden punched-out sores appear (possible eczema herpeticum).
sources: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) Atopic Dermatitis Guidelines

diseases.name: Impetigo
diseases.short_description: A highly contagious superficial bacterial skin infection, predominantly caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes, presenting with honey-colored crusted erosions.
common_characteristics: Classic non-bullous form with golden honey-colored adherence crusts
Bullous variant with flaccid, clear-to-turbid fluid-filled blisters
Erythematous base exposed upon detachment of superficial crusts
Commonly clustered around the perioral and perinasal areas of the face
Rapid spread via autoinoculation or direct physical contact
diagnostic_approaches: Clinical recognition of pathognomonic honey-colored crusted erosions
Bacterial Gram stain and wound culture with antibiotic sensitivity testing
Differential diagnosis against herpes simplex, contact dermatitis, and scabies
treatment_approaches: Topical prescription antibiotic ointment (mupirocin, retapamulin) for localized lesions
Oral beta-lactamase resistant antibiotics (cephalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate) for widespread lesions
Gentle debridement of crusts using warm soapy soaks before ointment application
Strict hygiene measures: daily hot laundry of towels and clothes, frequent handwashing
diseases.when_to_seek_care: Seek prompt healthcare consultation for definitive prescription antimicrobial therapy to halt contagion and prevent post-streptococcal complications.
sources: Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) Skin Infection Guidelines
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Impetigo Resource

diseases.name: Psoriasis
diseases.short_description: A chronic, systemic immune-mediated inflammatory dermatosis characterized by keratinocyte hyperproliferation, manifesting as well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery-white scales.
common_characteristics: Sharply circumscribed erythematous plaques covered by silvery micaceous scale
Predilection for extensor surfaces (elbows, knees), scalp, and lumbosacral region
Auspitz sign (punctate bleeding upon gentle detachment of scales)
Koebner phenomenon (appearance of new psoriatic lesions along lines of trauma)
Nail changes (pitting, oil drop sign, onycholysis) in up to 50% of patients
diagnostic_approaches: Clinical morphologic assessment and PASI (Psoriasis Area & Severity Index) scoring
Screening for psoriatic arthritis (CASPAR criteria) in all psoriatic patients
Punch biopsy in atypical or erythrodermic variants to confirm epidermal hyperplasia
Cardiovascular and metabolic risk factor comorbidity assessment
treatment_approaches: Topical fixed-combination vitamin D analogues (calcipotriol) and potent corticosteroids
Narrowband UVB (NB-UVB) phototherapy or targeted excimer laser therapy
Conventional systemic agents (methotrexate, cyclosporine, acitretin)
Targeted biologic therapeutics (anti-TNF, anti-IL-17, anti-IL-23 monoclonal antibodies)
Keratolytic agents (salicylic acid) to facilitate topical medication penetration
diseases.when_to_seek_care: Seek specialist dermatological care for personalized treatment planning, if joint pain or stiffness occurs, or if psoriasis covers greater than 5% of body surface area.
sources: AAD-NPF Joint Guidelines of Care for the Management of Psoriasis

diseases.name: Ringworm (Tinea Corporis)
diseases.short_description: A superficial dermatophytosis of glabrous skin caused by keratinophilic fungi (Trichophyton, Microsporum, or Epidermophyton), presenting as annular erythematous scaly plaques with active expanding borders.
common_characteristics: Annular (ring-shaped) erythematous plaque with central clearing
Active, raised, scaly or vesicular advancing outer perimeter
Mild to intense pruritus localized to the active lesion edge
Transmission from infected pets (zoophilic), humans (anthropophilic), or soil
diagnostic_approaches: Potassium hydroxide (KOH) direct microscopic mount showing septate hyphae
Fungal culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar for definitive species identification
Wood lamp fluorescence examination for select microsporum infections
Clinical differentiation from annular psoriasis, pityriasis rosea, and erythema annulare
treatment_approaches: Topical allylamine antifungals (terbinafine) or imidazoles (clotrimazole, ketoconazole)
Application continued for 1–2 weeks past complete visible clinical clearance
Oral antifungal therapy (terbinafine, itraconazole) for extensive or refractory cases
STRICT WARNING: Avoid topical steroid creams alone (prevents tinea incognito)
Veterinary screening and treatment of household pets to prevent reinfection
diseases.when_to_seek_care: Consult a doctor if lesions fail to respond to over-the-counter antifungals within 2 weeks, spread rapidly, or if systemic symptoms emerge.
sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Fungal Diseases Resource
British Association of Dermatologists (BAD) Tinea Guidelines

diseases.name: Scabies
diseases.short_description: A contagious, intensely pruritic ectoparasitic dermatosis caused by the microscopic burrowing mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis, characterized by nocturnal itch and interdigital burrows.
common_characteristics: Severe, intractable pruritus, classically exacerbated at nighttime
Serpiginous, thread-like greyish-white cutaneous burrows (2–10 mm in length)
Erythematous papules, excoriations, and secondary bacterial impetiginization
Characteristic anatomic predilection: web spaces of fingers, flexor wrists, axillae, umbilicus, genitalia
Frequent history of itching in close family members or household cohabitants
diagnostic_approaches: Dermoscopy revealing the characteristic delta-wing jet sign of the female mite
Skin scraping of unexcoriated burrows with mineral oil microscopy for mites, ova, or scybala
Burrow ink test (pigment concentrates inside mite tunnel)
Clinical diagnosis based on characteristic distribution and nocturnal itching
treatment_approaches: Topical 5% permethrin cream applied from neck to toes, left on for 8–14 hours, repeated after 7 days
Oral ivermectin (200 mcg/kg) as two doses spaced 7–14 days apart
Simultaneous treatment of ALL household members and sexual partners, regardless of symptoms
Decontamination: laundering bedding, towels, and worn clothing in hot water (>60°C)
Oral antihistamines and bland moisturizers for post-scabetic itch (can persist 2–4 weeks)
diseases.when_to_seek_care: Seek immediate medical attention for prescription scabicide therapy. Contact tracing and simultaneous household treatment are mandatory to stop cyclical transmission.
sources: World Health Organization (WHO) Scabies Factsheet and Guidelines
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Scabies Protocol

diseases.name: Seborrheic Dermatitis
diseases.short_description: A common chronic, relapsing inflammatory disorder affecting sebum-rich cutaneous areas, linked to Malassezia yeast colonization, abnormal lipid composition, and individual susceptibility.
common_characteristics: Greasy, yellowish, adherent or bran-like scales over erythematous patches
Symmetrical involvement of scalp (dandruff), eyebrows, nasolabial folds, and chest
Mild to moderate pruritus, frequently fluctuating with seasons and stress
Infantile variant (cradle cap) typically self-limiting within first year of life
Adult form follows a chronic waxing-and-waning lifelong clinical course
diagnostic_approaches: Clinical morphological evaluation of characteristic scale texture and anatomical zones
Exclusion of psoriasis (sebopsoriasis overlap), contact dermatitis, and rosacea
Screening for underlying conditions in severe or sudden refractory cases (HIV, Parkinsonism)
treatment_approaches: Medicated antifungal shampoos (ketoconazole 2%, zinc pyrithione, selenium sulfide, ciclopirox)
Topical low-potency corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors for acute facial erythema
Keratolytic agents (salicylic acid, coal tar) to loosen thick adherent scalp crusts
Maintenance regimen with antifungal washes once weekly to prevent relapses
Avoidance of heavy oil-based hair pomades and harsh alcohol-containing toners
diseases.when_to_seek_care: Consult a dermatologist if over-the-counter medicated shampoos fail, facial redness becomes bothersome, or scalp scaling becomes painful or secondarily infected.
sources: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) Seborrheic Dermatitis Guide
National Eczema Association (NEA) Seborrheic Dermatitis Resource

diseases.name: Urticaria (Hives)
diseases.short_description: A vascular reaction of the dermis characterized by transient, intensely pruritic, erythematous edematous wheals that typically resolve within 24 hours without leaving residual marks.
common_characteristics: Circumscribed, raised erythematous wheals with central pallor and surrounding flare
Evanescent nature: individual wheals appear, migrate, and resolve within 24 hours
Intense pruritus (itching) or stinging/burning sensation
May be accompanied by deeper subcutaneous swelling (angioedema) in up to 40% of cases
Classified as acute (<6 weeks duration) or chronic spontaneous/inducible (>6 weeks)
diagnostic_approaches: Comprehensive clinical history focusing on triggers (infections, foods, medications, NSAIDs)
Evaluation of inducible physical stimuli (dermographism, cold, heat, pressure, exercise)
Complete blood count and inflammatory markers for chronic persistent urticaria
Emergency assessment to immediately rule out systemic anaphylactic features
treatment_approaches: First-line: Second-generation non-sedating oral H1 antihistamines (cetirizine, fexofenadine, bilastine)
Up-titration of non-sedating antihistamines up to 4-fold standard dose under medical supervision
Third-line biologic therapy (omalizumab, anti-IgE) for chronic spontaneous urticaria
Short rescue course of oral corticosteroids (3–5 days) only for severe acute exacerbations
EMERGENCY WARNING: Intramuscular epinephrine (auto-injector) for any signs of anaphylaxis
diseases.when_to_seek_care: EMERGENCY: Seek immediate emergency room care if hives are accompanied by throat tightness, difficulty breathing, tongue/lip swelling, or dizziness. Consult a doctor for hives lasting over 6 weeks.
sources: American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology (AAAAI) Urticaria Resource
